items.stem: A revision website states: “Everything in a photograph is shown at the same scale.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Objects in the background appear smaller than the same objects in the foreground.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A wind rose for Bangkok shows the number of days in one month on which the wind blew from each direction: N 3, NE 1, E 3, SE 3, S 0, SW 1, W 7, NW 3. There were 10 calm days. (a) State the prevailing wind direction. (b) Check that the data total 31 days.
A revision website states: “Buying FSC-certified timber can help reduce unsustainable logging.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Consumer demand for certified wood rewards sustainable forest managers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: At a sandstone cliff on the Black Sea coast, the cliff edge retreated 36 m between 2005 and 2025. (a) Suggest why the rate of retreat may not stay the same. (b) Explain why soft cliffs such as boulder clay retreat quickly.
items.answer: (a) Storms and sea-level rise may speed it up; new defences or a wider beach may slow it; slumping happens in sudden events rather than steadily. (b) Clay is weak and easily eroded by waves; rain saturates it, causing slumping; eroded material is easily washed away so the cliff base is not protected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each reason up to [2] (b) 1 mark weak rock; 1 mark slumping/weathering [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 3.2, a sketch map of a meandering river. A steep, eroding bank lies on the outside of one bend and a gently sloping beach of sand and gravel on the inside. Downstream, two meander loops almost meet across a narrow neck of land. (a) Explain what is likely to happen to the narrow neck of land in the future. (b) Draw and describe a cross-section from the river cliff to the slip-off slope.
items.answer: (a) Erosion on the outside bends will narrow the neck further; in a flood the river will cut through, forming a straight channel and later an ox-bow lake. (b) Steep cliff on one side, deepest water close to it, channel becoming shallow towards the gently sloping deposits on the other side (asymmetrical).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark erosion narrows; 1 mark cut-off in flood; 1 mark ox-bow [3] (b) 1 mark asymmetry; 1 mark labels [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.3 shows information about land use on the slopes of a composite volcano in a lower-income country. Below 600 m: rice terraces and villages, population density 900 people per km². 600-1500 m: coffee, vegetables and dairy cattle, 400 people per km². Above 1500 m: forest and tourist trails to the summit (2900 m). A geothermal power station lies at 1200 m. (a) Describe how land use changes with height. (b) Suggest why some people may refuse to leave when warnings are issued.
items.answer: (a) Below 600 m dense villages and rice terraces; 600-1500 m coffee, vegetables, dairy and geothermal power; above 1500 m forest and tourism. (b) Fear of losing livestock, crops and property to looting; previous false alarms; strong attachment to land; lack of transport or a place to go.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each zone up to [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that paper topographic maps are no longer needed now that people use digital mapping and satellite navigation. You may wish to consider: cost; remote areas.
items.answer: For: Digital maps update quickly, zoom in and out and show live information such as traffic. GPS gives an exact location without needing grid references. Against: Phones lose signal and battery in remote areas, so walkers and rescue teams still carry paper maps. Contours, symbols and scale are the same skills needed to read digital maps. Paper maps show a wide area at once for planning. Judgement: Digital tools have changed map use, but map skills and paper maps are still needed, especially in remote areas and emergencies.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: A school weather station in Doha recorded the following data. Mon: max 30 °C, min 18 °C, rain 3 mm. Tue: max 23 °C, min 18 °C, rain 22 mm. Wed: max 21 °C, min 10 °C, rain 0 mm. Thu: max 18 °C, min 7 °C, rain 12 mm. Fri: max 28 °C, min 14 °C, rain 0 mm. (a) Calculate the mean maximum temperature. (b) Identify the day with the largest diurnal temperature range and state the range. (c) Suggest why the diurnal range is often smaller on cloudy, wet days.
items.answer: (a) 24 °C (b) Fri, 14 °C (c) Cloud reflects incoming sunlight by day (cooler maximum) and traps outgoing heat at night (warmer minimum).

items.stem: Study Fig. 6.1, a Gersmehl nutrient cycle for the tropical rainforest. The biomass store is much larger than the litter and soil stores. Transfers from litter to soil and from soil to biomass are very large; losses occur by leaching and surface run-off. (a) Explain why the litter store is very small. (b) Explain why the transfer from soil to biomass is large.
items.answer: (a) Hot, wet conditions all year mean decomposers break litter down very quickly, so it does not build up. (b) Plants grow all year and their dense, shallow roots absorb nutrients as soon as they are released.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark rapid decomposition; 1 mark climate reason [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Students measured the profile of a beach beside a spit from the sea to the back of the beach in 6 sections each 5 m long. Slope angles (°): 3, 2, 8, 12, 12, 12. Mean pebble size (mm) for each section: 29, 40, 47, 55, 67, 73. (a) Describe how pebble size changes up the beach. (b) Explain why larger pebbles are found at the back of the beach.
items.answer: (a) Pebble size increases from 29 mm near the sea to 73 mm at the back of the beach. (b) Only powerful storm-wave swash can throw large pebbles high up the beach; the weak backwash cannot carry them back down.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark storm swash; 1 mark weak backwash [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Beach nourishment is a permanent solution.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Waves and longshore drift remove the added sand, so it must be repeated regularly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: In one year a drainage basin receives 1800 mm of precipitation. Evapotranspiration is 1080 mm and river run-off is 280 mm. The rest is added to storage (soil water and groundwater). Suggest how the figures would differ in a hot, forested basin.
items.answer: Evapotranspiration would be a larger share because of high temperatures and transpiration by trees; less run-off.
items.markingKey: 1 mark more evapotranspiration; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how planting trees can reduce desertification. (b) Explain why international cooperation is needed to protect rainforests.
items.answer: (a) Roots bind the soil and reduce wind erosion; shade reduces evaporation; leaves add organic matter; trees act as windbreaks. (b) Demand for beef, soya, palm oil and timber comes from other countries; forests store carbon and biodiversity for the whole world; poorer countries need funding (e.g. debt-for-nature swaps, REDD+).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [3] (b) 1 mark global demand; 1 mark global benefit/funding [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.2 is a cross-section of Eyjafjallajökull, Iceland, a composite volcano at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American plates move apart. It shows a central vent, a crater, alternate layers of ash and lava, and a secondary vent on the flank. A town of 40 000 people lies 8 km from the summit, and the authorities have set an exclusion zone of 15 km. (a) Describe two hazards the town could face in an eruption. (b) Explain why the volcano erupts explosively.
items.answer: (a) Ash fall collapsing roofs and damaging crops and lungs; pyroclastic flows; lahars along river valleys; volcanic bombs; gases. (b) Its magma is viscous and gas-rich; gas cannot escape easily, so pressure builds until it is released violently.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each hazard with brief description [2] (b) 1 mark viscous; 1 mark gas pressure [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.5 is a photograph of a coastline. In the foreground is a wide, rocky wave-cut platform exposed at low tide. In the middle distance a steep chalk cliff about 30 m high has a cave at its base and a narrow arch at the headland. In the background two isolated pillars of rock stand in the sea. Grass covers the cliff top, with a footpath close to the edge. (a) Identify two landforms of erosion shown in Fig. 1.5. (b) Draw a labelled sketch to show the main features of the coastline. (Describe what your sketch would include.)
items.answer: (a) Any two: cliff, wave-cut platform, cave, arch, stack. (b) Outline of the cliff and headland; labels and annotations for wave-cut platform, cave, arch and stacks; sea and cliff-top path; title and direction of view.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark outline; 2 marks labelled features [3]

items.stem: Fig. 5.2 is a climate graph for Kisangani, DR Congo (0.5° N). Temperature (°C): Jan 25.4, Feb 25.7, Mar 25.8, Apr 25.8, May 25.6, Jun 25, Jul 24.3, Aug 24.4, Sep 24.8, Oct 25, Nov 25.1, Dec 25. Precipitation (mm): Jan 80, Feb 110, Mar 160, Apr 170, May 160, Jun 110, Jul 120, Aug 160, Sep 180, Oct 220, Nov 190, Dec 110. (a) Calculate the annual temperature range. (b) Identify the wettest month and its rainfall. (c) Describe the main features of the climate shown in Fig. 5.2.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 °C (b) October, 220 mm (c) Hot all year (24.3-25.8 °C) with a very small annual range of 1.5 °C; heavy rain (1770 mm a year) with rain in every month, wettest in October.
items.markingKey: (a) 25.8 (March) − 24.3 = 1.5 °C [1] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark temperature with data; 1 mark range; 1 mark rainfall total/distribution [3]

items.stem: With reference to the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India, or another example of a coral reef or mangrove ecosystem you have studied, explain the threats to the ecosystem.
items.answer: Model answer (the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India): Clearance for shrimp farming and rice; sea-level rise and increasing salinity; cyclones; pollution from shipping and industry; over-harvesting.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Natural and human threats (warming, bleaching, pollution, clearance, sea-level rise) with explanation. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Table 3.1 shows measurements at five sites downstream along a river. Site 1 (0 km from source): width 1.7 m, mean pebble size 166 mm. Site 2 (4 km from source): width 1.8 m, mean pebble size 127 mm. Site 3 (9 km from source): width 2.8 m, mean pebble size 133 mm. Site 4 (15 km from source): width 3.8 m, mean pebble size 123 mm. Site 5 (22 km from source): width 5.1 m, mean pebble size 73 mm. (a) Describe how channel width changes downstream. Use data. (b) Describe how pebble size changes downstream. (c) Suggest a reason for the anomaly in pebble size.
items.answer: (a) Width increases from 1.7 m at Site 1 to 5.1 m at Site 5. (b) Pebble size generally decreases from 166 mm to 73 mm, except at Site 3 where it is larger than upstream. (c) A tributary or eroding bank may have added fresh, larger material at that site; or the sample was too small.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark trend; 1 mark data/anomaly [2] (c) 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Table 6.1 shows the percentage of nutrients stored in the biomass, litter and soil. Tropical rainforest: biomass 65%, litter 3%, soil ?. A temperate grassland: biomass 10%, litter 5%, soil 85%. (a) Calculate the percentage stored in the rainforest soil. (b) The rainforest data are to be drawn as a pie chart. Calculate the angle of the biomass sector. (c) Suggest why farmers who clear rainforest find that yields fall after a few years.
items.answer: (a) 32% (b) 234° (c) Once the biomass is removed, nutrients are no longer recycled; heavy rain leaches the thin soil, so fertility falls quickly.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 − 65 − 3 = 32% [1] (b) 65 × 3.6 = 234° [1] (c) 1 mark loss of store; 1 mark leaching [2]

items.stem: At the Sunda Trench south of Java, Indonesia, the Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates move together at about 6 cm per year. (a) Calculate how far the plates move in 5 000 000 years. Give your answer in km. (b) Describe the landforms and hazards found at this type of boundary.
items.answer: (a) 300 km (b) An ocean trench, explosive composite volcanoes and powerful earthquakes at a range of depths; tsunamis can occur.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Lava flows are usually the deadliest volcanic hazard.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Most lava flows are slow enough to walk away from; pyroclastic flows and lahars kill far more people.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 5.1 shows weather readings at 09:00 for six days. Day 1: pressure 1018 mb, rain 0 mm, cloud 1 oktas. Day 2: pressure 1012 mb, rain 0 mm, cloud 3 oktas. Day 3: pressure 1003 mb, rain 8 mm, cloud 6 oktas. Day 4: pressure 994 mb, rain 28 mm, cloud 8 oktas. Day 5: pressure 998 mb, rain 8 mm, cloud 4 oktas. Day 6: pressure 1004 mb, rain 0 mm, cloud 3 oktas. Describe the changes in air pressure over the six days.
items.answer: Pressure fell from 1018 mb to a low of 994 mb on Day 4, then rose to 1004 mb.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fall then rise; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: Put these statements about the formation of a levee into the correct order. P: The river floods and spreads over the flood plain. Q: The coarsest sediment is deposited closest to the river. R: Velocity falls suddenly at the edge of the channel. S: Finer silt is carried further and deposited on the flood plain. T: Repeated floods build up raised banks.
items.answer: P, R, Q, S, T
items.markingKey: Correct order P, R, Q, S, T. 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if one pair reversed. [2]

items.stem: Table 6.1 shows the percentage of nutrients stored in the biomass, litter and soil. Tropical rainforest: biomass 65%, litter 2%, soil ?. A temperate deciduous forest: biomass 45%, litter 10%, soil 45%. (a) Explain why so little is stored in the rainforest litter. (b) The rainforest data are to be drawn as a pie chart. Calculate the angle of the biomass sector. (c) Suggest why farmers who clear rainforest find that yields fall after a few years.
items.answer: (a) Decomposition is very rapid in the hot, wet climate. (b) 234° (c) Once the biomass is removed, nutrients are no longer recycled; heavy rain leaches the thin soil, so fertility falls quickly.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 65 × 3.6 = 234° [1] (c) 1 mark loss of store; 1 mark leaching [2]

items.stem: “Wave type is the most important factor affecting the rate of coastal erosion.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: fetch; rock type.
items.answer: For: Destructive waves with long fetch and storms cause rapid erosion. Against: Rock type and structure matter: soft boulder clay at Holderness erodes about 2 m a year while granite erodes very slowly. Beaches absorb wave energy; human defences and sub-aerial processes also affect rates. Judgement: Wave energy drives erosion, but geology often determines how fast it happens.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 is a line graph showing the annual rainfall at Lagos (mm). The values plotted are: 2017: 635, 2018: 554, 2019: 716, 2020: 852, 2021: 893, 2022: 868, 2023: 922. (a) Describe the trend shown by Fig. 1.3. Use data in your answer. (b) Calculate the percentage change between 2017 and 2023.
items.answer: (a) Overall an increase from 635 mm (2017) to 922 mm (2023), with fluctuations; highest 922 mm in 2023, lowest 554 mm in 2018. (b) +45.2%
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark overall trend; 1 mark change in rate/fluctuation; 1 mark data with units [3] (b) (922 − 635) ÷ 635 × 100 = 45.2% [2]

items.stem: “Secondary effects of earthquakes are more serious than primary effects.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: long-term economic effects; Haiti 2010; Nepal 2015.
items.answer: For: Tōhoku (2011): the tsunami caused over 90% of deaths and the Fukushima nuclear accident. Haiti (2010): cholera killed thousands in the months after. Against: In Nepal (2015) and Haiti most deaths came from buildings collapsing during the shaking. Primary effects destroy the infrastructure needed for recovery. Judgement: It depends on the event: for coastal subduction earthquakes secondary effects are often worse; for inland earthquakes primary effects usually dominate.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows air temperatures recorded over 24 hours in July at a weather station in the Sahara: 03:00 11 °C, 06:00 9 °C, 09:00 14 °C, 12:00 22 °C, 15:00 25 °C, 18:00 20 °C, 21:00 13 °C, 24:00 12 °C. The sky was cloudless. (a) State the times of the highest and lowest temperatures. (b) Explain why the temperature range is so large. (c) Explain why the highest temperature occurs in the afternoon rather than at noon.
items.answer: (a) Highest at 15:00 (25 °C); lowest at 06:00 (9 °C). (b) Cloudless skies let intense sunshine heat the bare ground by day; at night heat radiates quickly to space because there is no cloud or water vapour to trap it. (c) The ground keeps absorbing more heat than it loses until mid-afternoon, and heats the air above it after a delay.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark day; 1 mark night [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Students measured the River Tees at Site 3, in the middle course. Width = 1.8 m, mean depth = 0.25 m. A float took 8 s to travel 5 m. (a) Calculate the velocity in m/s. (b) Suggest why surface float velocity may be higher than the mean velocity. (c) Suggest one way of making the velocity measurement more reliable.
items.answer: (a) 0.62 m/s (b) Friction with the bed and banks slows water near them, so surface water in mid-channel flows fastest. (c) Repeat the float timing three times and take the mean; use a flow meter; avoid windy conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) 5 ÷ 8 = 0.62 m/s [1] (b) 1 mark friction; 1 mark surface fastest [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Table 6.1 shows the percentage of nutrients stored in the biomass, litter and soil. Tropical rainforest: biomass 75%, litter 2%, soil ?. A coniferous (taiga) forest: biomass 25%, litter 50%, soil 25%. (a) Calculate the percentage stored in the rainforest soil. (b) The rainforest data are to be drawn as a pie chart. Calculate the angle of the biomass sector. (c) Suggest why farmers who clear rainforest find that yields fall after a few years.
items.answer: (a) 23% (b) 270° (c) Once the biomass is removed, nutrients are no longer recycled; heavy rain leaches the thin soil, so fertility falls quickly.
items.markingKey: (a) 100 − 75 − 2 = 23% [1] (b) 75 × 3.6 = 270° [1] (c) 1 mark loss of store; 1 mark leaching [2]
